title: Proposed Immigration Court Contempt Rule Would Fine Lawyers Who Allege Bias
excerpt: EOIR's proposed contempt penalties of up to $3,500 would cover private attorneys, respondents, and witnesses but exempt government attorneys. AILA urges withdrawal; supporters say judges have lacked an accountability tool since 1996.
body:
• A Department of Justice proposed rule published July 30, 2026, would let immigration judges impose civil money penalties of up to $3,500 for contempt, covering private attorneys, respondents, and non-government witnesses.
  • Critics including the American Immigration Lawyers Association say the rule would increase bias in immigration court because it exempts government attorneys and witnesses, and because it treats language that "unfairly maligns" a judge's impartiality as punishable abusive language.
  • What this means for you: the rule is not in effect and no fines can be imposed today. If you have a pending case, your lawyer's ability to raise a bias claim on the record is at stake, because that claim is often how an appeal is preserved.
  • Supporters say judges have lacked a direct accountability tool since Congress authorized contempt penalties in 1996, in a system with more than 3.5 million pending cases.

A proposed rule from the Executive Office for Immigration Review would give immigration judges a new power to fine people who appear before them, and immigrant advocates say the way that power is drawn would increase bias against people in immigration court.

The proposal, titled "Civil Money Penalty for Actions in Contempt of an Immigration Judge's Proper Exercise of Authority," was published July 30, 2026, according to the Justice Department's EOIR Federal Register notices. It would implement an Immigration and Nationality Act provision authorizing judges to sanction contempt by civil money penalty. Comments were due September 28, 2026.

What the rule would punish

The rule covers five kinds of conduct: repeated failure to appear on time without good cause; repeated failure to meet filing deadlines; disorderly or abusive behavior or language in court and abusive language in any filing; knowingly or recklessly making a false statement or offering false evidence; and willfully misleading or threatening any person about a case. America First Legal, which supports the rule, puts the maximum penalty at up to $3,500.

https://x.com/randyferrell/status/2112335516557271491

The proposal includes a warning in most cases, a notice of intent, review involving the Chief Immigration Judge, and an appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals, according to Lal Legal's analysis of the text.

The bias objection: who is covered, and what speech counts

The American Immigration Lawyers Association submitted a comment on September 25, 2026, opposing the rule and urging EOIR to withdraw it in its entirety. AILA's central point is asymmetry: the rule "would allow immigration judges to impose monetary penalties on private attorneys, clients, and witnesses" while it "exempts penalties from being applied to government attorneys and witnesses." The National Immigration Project makes the same point in its resource listing on the July 30 rule.

The second objection is about speech. The definition of abusive language includes language that "impugns the integrity of the court" or "unfairly maligns the competence or impartiality" of a judge, according to Lal Legal. A lawyer who believes a judge prejudged a case must allege bias to preserve it for appeal. Critics argue that if the criticized judge can initiate a sanction over whether criticism was "unfair," lawyers will soften or omit bias claims, and appellate issues will be lost.

"For too long, members of the private immigration bar have been able to treat hearing dates, filing deadlines, and court orders as optional because immigration judges lacked a direct way to hold them accountable."

— Alexandra Dunn, Attorney, America First Legal

The case for the rule

Supporters answer that the authority is not new, only unused. Congress authorized contempt penalties in 1996, but the Justice Department never adopted the regulations to make it usable, according to America First Legal. AFL argues judges are left with disciplinary referrals that can take years, while hearings are postponed when attorneys fail to appear, in a system with more than 3.5 million cases.

AFL says the rule gives judges a direct tool against repeated misconduct and holds private attorneys to standards of candor and compliance. Government attorneys sit outside the regime; DOJ's explanation, as summarized by Lal Legal, is reluctance to have one executive agency fine lawyers employed by another.

What this means for people in court now

Immigration judges are not independent Article III judges. They are attorneys employed by the Department of Justice, appointed by the Attorney General, and the government prosecutor also works for the executive branch. Critics say a rule that deters challenges to a judge's impartiality, while exempting government lawyers, tilts an already tilted field.

Nothing changes in a hearing today. EOIR must review the comments filed, including AILA's opposition and America First Legal's support, before issuing a final rule through the regulations.gov rulemaking process. If you are in removal proceedings, discuss with your attorney how bias and due-process objections are documented on the record, since a final rule could affect how forcefully those objections are made.
